Anatomy-05.question: ১) Payers patches are predominantly found in
২) Most numerous main glands of prostate are contained within
৩) Uterine artery is a branch of which artery?
Anatomy-05.exp:
The uterine artery is a branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery.

  • It supplies the uterus, cervix, upper vagina, and uterine tubes.

  • It crosses over the ureter near the cervix (“water under the bridge”):

    • Uterine artery = bridge

    • Ureter = water

Why other options are incorrect:

  • External iliac: Gives branches mainly to the lower limb (continues as femoral artery).

  • Internal iliac:  Gives uterine artery through its anterior division.

  • Pudendal:  A branch of internal iliac; supplies perineum, not the uterus.

  • Femoral:  Supplies lower limb.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Uterine artery → Anterior division of internal iliac artery

  • Ovarian artery → Abdominal aorta

  • Uterine artery crosses ureter → “Water under the bridge”

Exam Pearl:
Uterine artery is a branch of the internal iliac artery and is clinically important during hysterectomy due to its relation with the ureter.

Anatomy-05.question: ৪) Somatostatin is secreted from which cell?
৫) Urethra passes through which part of penis?
৬) Dominant hormone in proliferative stage of menstrual cycle
৭) Homologus structure of penis in female
৮) The classic hepatic lobule emphasizes
Anatomy-05.exp:
The classic hepatic lobule is the structural and functional unit of the liver that emphasizes the exocrine function of hepatocytes, particularly the production and flow of bile.

  • Hepatocytes are arranged in plates around a central vein.

  • Bile flows from hepatocytes → bile canaliculi → bile ducts (opposite direction to blood flow).

  • This model highlights bile secretion and exocrine activity.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Endocrine function of hepatocyte: Better represented by the hepatic acinus, which emphasizes metabolic exchange between blood and hepatocytes.

  • Oxygen content of blood: Mainly emphasized by the hepatic acinus (Rappaport model), showing oxygen gradients.

  • Nutrient content of blood: Also related to the hepatic acinus, which describes metabolic zones.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Liver model Main emphasis
Classic hepatic lobule Bile secretion (exocrine function)
Portal lobule Exocrine bile drainage
Hepatic acinus Blood supply, oxygen & metabolic gradients

Exam Pearl:
Classic hepatic lobule → bile flow/exocrine function; Hepatic acinus → oxygen and nutrient gradients.

Anatomy-05.question: ৯) Accessory digestive organs exclude
১০) Not a part of pharynx
১১) Oesophagus ends at
১২) Innermost muscular layer of stomach
১৩) Inlet of inguinal canal situated in-
Anatomy-05.exp:
The deep (internal) inguinal ring, which is the inlet of the inguinal canal, is an opening in the fascia transversalis.

  • It lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.

  • It allows passage of the spermatic cord (male) or round ligament of uterus (female) into the inguinal canal.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Parietal peritoneum: Forms the lining of the abdominal cavity; not the site of the deep inguinal ring.

  • Fascia transversalis:  Contains the deep inguinal ring (inlet).

  • Internal oblique:  Forms part of the roof and contributes to the conjoint tendon, but does not contain the inlet.

  • External oblique:  Contains the superficial inguinal ring (outlet).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Structure Location
Deep inguinal ring (inlet) Fascia transversalis
Superficial inguinal ring (outlet) External oblique aponeurosis
Inguinal canal roof Internal oblique + transversus abdominis
Posterior wall Fascia transversalis + conjoint tendon

Exam Pearl:
Deep inguinal ring = opening in fascia transversalis; superficial ring = external oblique aponeurosis.

Anatomy-05.question: ১৪) Inferior venacava passes through—
Anatomy-05.exp:
The inferior vena cava (IVC) passes through the caval opening of the diaphragm, which is an osseoaponeurotic opening.

  • Level: T8 vertebra

  • Location: Right central tendon of diaphragm

  • The opening is formed mainly by the tendinous part (central tendon) of the diaphragm.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Muscular opening: The oesophagus passes through the muscular opening (T10).

  • Tendinous opening:  Although the caval opening is in the tendon, the standard classification is osseoaponeurotic opening.

  • Aponeurotic opening:  Not the accepted term for the caval opening.

  • Osseoaponeurotic opening:  Correct for IVC.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Structure Diaphragm opening Level
IVC Caval opening (osseoaponeurotic) T8
Oesophagus Muscular opening T10
Aorta Arcuate ligament (aponeurotic) T12

Exam Pearl:
IVC → T8 → caval opening → central tendon (osseoaponeurotic).

Anatomy-05.question: ১৫) Abdominal aorta begins at the level of
Anatomy-05.exp:
The abdominal aorta begins at the level of T12 vertebra when the thoracic aorta passes through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm.

  • Aortic hiatus: T12 level

  • It continues downward in the abdomen and ends by bifurcating into the right and left common iliac arteries at the level of L4.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • T11: Not the level of aortic hiatus.

  • T12: Beginning of abdominal aorta.

  • L4: Site of bifurcation of abdominal aorta.

  • L5:  Not a major landmark for the aorta.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Structure Vertebral level
Aortic hiatus → T12 Abdominal aorta begins
Oesophageal hiatus → T10 Oesophagus passes diaphragm
Caval opening → T8 IVC passes diaphragm
Aortic bifurcation → L4 Common iliac arteries

Exam Pearl:
Abdominal aorta begins at T12 and bifurcates at L4.

Anatomy-05.question: ১৬) Continuation of abdominal aorta
Anatomy-05.exp:
The abdominal aorta terminates by bifurcating into the right and left common iliac arteries at the level of L4 vertebra.

  • The common iliac arteries are the direct continuation of the abdominal aorta and supply the pelvis and lower limbs.

  • Each common iliac artery divides into:

    • Internal iliac artery → pelvis

    • External iliac artery → lower limb

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Common iliac artery:  Terminal continuation of abdominal aorta.

  • Median sacral artery:  A small midline branch arising from the posterior aspect of the aorta near its bifurcation.

  • Internal iliac artery: Branch of common iliac artery.

  • External iliac artery:  Branch of common iliac artery that continues as femoral artery.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Abdominal aorta begins: T12

  • Abdominal aorta ends: L4

  • Termination: Right & left common iliac arteries

Exam Pearl:
Abdominal aorta → Common iliac arteries → Internal + External iliac arteries.

Anatomy-05.question: ১৭) Type of vena caval opening -
Anatomy-05.exp:
The vena caval opening (caval opening) of the diaphragm is an osseoaponeurotic opening.

  • It transmits the inferior vena cava (IVC).

  • Located at the level of T8 vertebra.

  • It lies in the central tendon (tendinous part) of the diaphragm.

  • The opening enlarges during inspiration due to stretching of the central tendon.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Muscular:  The oesophageal hiatus is a muscular opening (T10).

  • Aponeurotic:  Not the standard classification for caval opening.

  • Tendinous:  Although it lies in the central tendon, the accepted term is osseoaponeurotic.

  • Osseoaponeurotic:  Correct classification for IVC opening.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Diaphragmatic opening Type Level Structure
Caval opening Osseoaponeurotic T8 IVC
Oesophageal hiatus Muscular T10 Oesophagus
Aortic hiatus Aponeurotic T12 Aorta

Exam Pearl:
IVC passes through the T8 caval opening, an osseoaponeurotic opening in the diaphragm.

Anatomy-05.question: ১৮) Structure passing through esophageal opening –
Anatomy-05.exp:
The oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm (at T10 level) transmits:

  • Oesophagus

  • Anterior and posterior vagal trunks (both vagus nerves)

The vagal trunks accompany the oesophagus through the diaphragm and contribute to the autonomic supply of the stomach.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Thoracic duct:  Passes through the aortic hiatus (T12).

  • Right phrenic nerve:  Mainly passes through the caval opening or pierces the diaphragm separately.

  • Left phrenic nerve:  Pierces the diaphragm separately; not through the oesophageal hiatus.

  • Both vagus:  Pass through the oesophageal hiatus.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Diaphragm opening Level Structures
Caval opening T8 IVC + right phrenic nerve (variable)
Oesophageal hiatus T10 Oesophagus + vagal trunks
Aortic hiatus T12 Aorta + thoracic duct

Exam Pearl:
Oesophageal hiatus = Oesophagus + both vagal trunks at T10.

Anatomy-05.question: ১৯) Content of deep perineal pouch –
Anatomy-05.exp:
The deep perineal pouch contains structures related to the urogenital diaphragm and includes:

  • Membranous urethra (male)

  • Proximal part of urethra (female)

  • External urethral sphincter

  • Deep transverse perineal muscle

  • Bulbourethral glands (male)

  • Neurovascular structures

Therefore, urethra is a content of the deep perineal pouch.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Crus penis:  Located in the superficial perineal pouch (attached to ischiopubic ramus).

  • Crus clitoris:  Located in the superficial perineal pouch.

  • Urethra:  Present in deep perineal pouch.

  • Bartholin gland (greater vestibular gland):  Located in the superficial perineal pouch.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Deep perineal pouch Superficial perineal pouch
Membranous urethra Crus penis/clitoris
External urethral sphincter Bulb of penis/clitoris
Deep transverse perineal muscle Greater vestibular gland (Bartholin)

Exam Pearl:
Deep perineal pouch contains the urethra; superficial pouch contains erectile tissues and Bartholin glands.

Anatomy-05.question: ২০) Gastric glands lies in-
Anatomy-05.exp:
Gastric glands are located in the lamina propria of the gastric mucosa.

The stomach wall layers (from inner to outer):

  1. Mucosa

    • Epithelium

    • Lamina propria (contains gastric glands)

    • Muscularis mucosae

  2. Submucosa

  3. Muscularis propria

  4. Serosa

Gastric glands contain cells such as:

  • Parietal cells → HCl and intrinsic factor

  • Chief cells → Pepsinogen

  • Mucous cells → Mucus

  • G cells → Gastrin

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Muscularis propria:  Contains smooth muscle layers responsible for gastric movements.

  • Submucosa:  Contains blood vessels, lymphatics, and connective tissue.

  • Muscularis mucosa:  Thin muscle layer separating mucosa from submucosa.

  • Lamina propria:  Contains gastric glands.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Gastric glands → Lamina propria of mucosa

  • Brunner glands → Submucosa of duodenum

  • Crypts of Lieberkühn → Intestinal mucosa

Exam Pearl:
Gastric glands are embedded in the lamina propria of the gastric mucosa.

Anatomy-05.question: ২১) Main artery of stomach
Anatomy-05.exp:
The left gastric artery is considered the main artery of the stomach.

  • It is the largest direct branch of the coeliac trunk.

  • It supplies the upper lesser curvature of the stomach.

  • It anastomoses with the right gastric artery along the lesser curvature.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Right gastric artery:  Supplies the lower part of lesser curvature; usually a branch of the hepatic artery.

  • Left gastro-epiploic (gastro-omental) artery:  Supplies the greater curvature; branch of splenic artery.

  • Splenic artery:  Supplies the stomach indirectly through short gastric and left gastro-epiploic branches.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Artery Origin Supply
Left gastric Coeliac trunk Main artery of stomach, lesser curvature
Right gastric Hepatic artery Lesser curvature
Left gastro-omental Splenic artery Greater curvature
Right gastro-omental Gastroduodenal artery Greater curvature

Exam Pearl:
Left gastric artery (branch of coeliac trunk) is the main arterial supply of the stomach.

Anatomy-05.question: ২২) Most dilated part of GIT—
Anatomy-05.exp:
The stomach is the most dilated part of the gastrointestinal tract (GIT).

  • It is a J-shaped, expandable organ located between the oesophagus and duodenum.

  • It acts as a reservoir for food and allows mechanical digestion and mixing.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Rectum: A dilated part of the large intestine for temporary storage of feces, but not the most dilated part of GIT.

  • Sigmoid colon:  A curved segment of colon, not the most dilated.

  • Anus: Terminal opening of the GIT, not a dilated part.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most dilated part of GIT → Stomach

  • Longest part of GIT → Small intestine

  • Largest digestive gland → Liver

  • Largest lymphoid organ → Spleen

Exam Pearl:
Stomach is the most dilated portion of the entire gastrointestinal tract.

Anatomy-05.question: ২৩) Content of lesser omentum—
Anatomy-05.exp:
The lesser omentum (especially the hepatoduodenal ligament) contains the portal triad:

  1. Common bile duct (CBD) — right side

  2. Proper hepatic artery — left side

  3. Portal vein — posteriorly

Among the given options, CBD is a content of the lesser omentum.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Left gastric artery:  Runs along the lesser curvature of the stomach but is not a content of the lesser omentum.

  • Portal vein:  Also present in the lesser omentum (portal triad), but in MCQ single-best-answer format, CBD is a classic content.

  • Hepatic artery:  Proper hepatic artery is also part of the portal triad within the lesser omentum.

  • CBD:  Classic content of hepatoduodenal ligament.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:
Portal triad in hepatoduodenal ligament:

  • Bile duct (CBD) → Right

  • Hepatic artery → Left

  • Portal vein → Posterior

Exam Pearl:
Lesser omentum contains the portal triad: CBD + hepatic artery + portal vein.

Anatomy-05.question: ২৪) Mucous gland of duodenum lies in
Anatomy-05.exp:
The mucous glands of the duodenum are called Brunner’s glands, and they are located in the submucosa.

Functions of Brunner’s glands:

  • Secrete alkaline mucus

  • Neutralize acidic chyme entering from the stomach

  • Protect duodenal mucosa from gastric acid

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Mucosa: Contains intestinal glands (crypts of Lieberkühn), not Brunner’s glands.

  • Lamina propria:  Contains connective tissue, immune cells, and vessels within mucosa.

  • Submucosa:  Contains Brunner’s glands.

  • Muscularis mucosa: Thin muscle layer separating mucosa from submucosa.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Structure Location
Brunner’s glands Duodenal submucosa
Gastric glands Lamina propria of stomach mucosa
Crypts of Lieberkühn Intestinal mucosa

Exam Pearl:
Brunner’s glands = duodenum + submucosa + alkaline mucus secretion.

Anatomy-05.question: ২৫) Circular fold absent in—
Anatomy-05.exp:
Circular folds (plicae circulares / valves of Kerckring) are permanent folds of the small intestine mucosa and submucosa that increase the surface area for absorption.

They are:

  • Present in the duodenum (except the first part)

  • Prominent in the jejunum

  • Reduced in the ileum

They are absent in the colon.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Proximal part of duodenum:  First part is relatively smooth, but other parts of duodenum have circular folds.

  • Proximal part of jejunum:  Has prominent circular folds.

  • Proximal part of ileum:  May have circular folds, though less prominent.

  • Proximal part of colon:  Circular folds are absent.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most prominent plicae circulares → Jejunum

  • Absent → First part of duodenum and colon

  • Small intestine → Circular folds for absorption

Exam Pearl:
Plicae circulares are a feature of small intestine, not colon.

Anatomy-05.question: ২৬) Appendicular artery is a branch of
Anatomy-05.exp:
The appendicular artery is a branch of the ileocolic artery, which is a branch of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA).

  • The appendicular artery runs through the mesoappendix to supply the appendix.

  • It is usually an end artery, so obstruction can lead to appendicular ischemia and gangrene.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Right colic artery: Supplies ascending colon; not the main supply of appendix.

  • Middle colic artery: Supplies transverse colon.

  • Left colic artery:  Branch of inferior mesenteric artery; supplies descending colon.

  • Ileocolic artery:  Gives the appendicular artery.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Artery Branch of Supply
Appendicular artery Ileocolic artery (SMA) Appendix
Right colic artery SMA Ascending colon
Middle colic artery SMA Transverse colon
Left colic artery IMA Descending colon

Exam Pearl:
Appendix blood supply = appendicular artery → branch of ileocolic artery → SMA.

Anatomy-05.question: ২৭) Most common position of appendix -
Anatomy-05.exp:
The most common position of the vermiform appendix is retrocecal (retrocolic).

  • The appendix lies behind the caecum in about 60–65% of individuals.

  • This position may make appendicitis symptoms less obvious because the inflamed appendix is away from the parietal peritoneum.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Preileal:  Appendix lies anterior to ileum; less common.

  • Postileal:  Appendix lies posterior to ileum; uncommon.

  • Retro-cecal:  Most common position.

  • Sub-cecal:  Appendix lies below the caecum; less common.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:
Positions of appendix (common to rare):

  1. Retrocecal/retrocolic (~65%) ⭐

  2. Pelvic

  3. Subcecal

  4. Preileal

  5. Postileal

Exam Pearl:
Most common appendix position = retrocecal (behind the caecum).

Anatomy-05.question: ২৮) Principal artery of Rectum—
Anatomy-05.exp:
The superior rectal artery is the principal artery supplying the rectum.

  • It is the continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA).

  • It supplies the upper and middle parts of the rectum.

  • It divides into two branches that descend on either side of the rectum.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Superior rectal artery:  Main arterial supply of rectum.

  • Middle rectal artery:  Branch of internal iliac artery; supplies lower rectum.

  • Median sacral artery:  Small midline branch from abdominal aorta; minor supply.

  • Inferior rectal artery:  Branch of internal pudendal artery; supplies anal canal and lower rectum.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Artery Origin Supply
Superior rectal artery Inferior mesenteric artery Main supply of rectum
Middle rectal artery Internal iliac artery Lower rectum
Inferior rectal artery Internal pudendal artery Anal canal

Exam Pearl:
Principal artery of rectum = Superior rectal artery (continuation of IMA).

Anatomy-05.question: ২৯) Hirschsprung disease usually occur in—
Anatomy-05.exp:
Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon) most commonly affects the rectosigmoid region, especially the sigmoid colon.

Pathogenesis:

  • Failure of migration of neural crest cells → absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach) and submucosal (Meissner) plexuses.

  • This causes failure of relaxation of the affected segment → functional obstruction and proximal megacolon.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Appendix:  Not a typical site.

  • Sigmoid colon:  Most common site (rectosigmoid involvement).

  • Descending colon:  May be involved in extensive disease but less common.

  • Transverse colon:  Rare involvement.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Hirschsprung disease → Aganglionosis

  • Most common site → Rectosigmoid

  • Defect → Neural crest cell migration failure

  • Cells absent → Ganglion cells of Auerbach & Meissner plexus

Exam Pearl:
Hirschsprung disease most commonly involves the rectosigmoid colon due to absence of enteric ganglion cells.

Anatomy-05.question: ৩০) Which vein drain into portal system—
Anatomy-05.exp:
The superior rectal vein drains into the portal venous system.

Venous drainage of rectum:

  • Superior rectal vein → Inferior mesenteric vein → Splenic vein → Portal vein (portal system)

  • Middle rectal vein → Internal iliac vein → Inferior vena cava (systemic circulation)

  • Inferior rectal vein → Internal pudendal vein → Internal iliac vein → IVC (systemic circulation)

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Superior rectal vein:  Drains into portal system.

  • Middle rectal vein:  Drains into systemic circulation.

  • Both superior & middle rectal veins:  Only superior rectal vein is portal.

  • Inferior rectal vein:  Drains into systemic circulation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:
Portosystemic anastomosis at rectum:

  • Superior rectal vein → Portal system

  • Middle & inferior rectal veins → Systemic system

Clinical importance:

  • Portal hypertension → hemorrhoids due to dilation of rectal venous plexus.

Exam Pearl:
Superior rectal vein = portal drainage; middle and inferior rectal veins = systemic drainage.

Anatomy-05.question: ৩১) Anus below the pectinate develops from—
Anatomy-05.exp:
The anus below the pectinate line develops from the proctodeum (an ectodermal structure).

The pectinate line represents the junction between:

  • Above pectinate line: Endoderm-derived (hindgut) → visceral innervation, portal drainage

  • Below pectinate line: Ectoderm-derived (proctodeum) → somatic innervation, systemic drainage

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Stomodium: Primitive mouth region; forms oral cavity structures.

  • Proctodeum:  Forms the lower anal canal and anus below the pectinate line.

  • Urogenital sinus:  Forms parts of urinary and genital systems.

  • Urorectal sinus: Related to cloacal division during development, not the direct origin of lower anus.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Region Embryological origin
Above pectinate line Endoderm (hindgut)
Below pectinate line Ectoderm (proctodeum)

Exam Pearl:
Below pectinate line = proctodeum (ectodermal origin).

Anatomy-05.question: ৩২) Most dependent part of abdomen in lying position -
Anatomy-05.exp:
In the supine (lying) position, the most dependent part of the peritoneal cavity is the hepato-renal pouch (Morrison’s pouch).

  • It is the space between the right lobe of the liver and the right kidney.

  • Fluid (blood, pus, ascites) tends to collect here in a patient lying on the back.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Pelvic cavity:  It is the most dependent part when a person is standing, not lying.

  • Iliac fossa:  Not the lowest point in the supine position.

  • Hepato-renal pouch:  Most dependent peritoneal recess in supine position.

  • Greater sac:  A large general peritoneal compartment, not the most dependent part.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Supine position → Hepato-renal pouch (Morrison’s pouch)

  • Standing position → Pelvic cavity (rectovesical pouch/rectouterine pouch)

Exam Pearl:
Morrison’s pouch is the most dependent part of the abdomen in a lying (supine) position.

Anatomy-05.question: ৩৩) True ligament of liver—
Anatomy-05.exp:
The true ligaments of the liver are remnants of fetal vascular structures that contain fibrous tissue.

Examples:

  • Ligamentum venosum → remnant of ductus venosus

  • Ligamentum teres hepatis → remnant of umbilical vein

Among the given options, ligamentum venosum is a true ligament of the liver.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Falciform ligament:  A peritoneal fold (false ligament); contains ligamentum teres in its free margin.

  • Coronary ligament:  A peritoneal reflection attaching liver to diaphragm (false ligament).

  • Ligamentum venosum: True fibrous remnant of fetal circulation.

  • Lesser omentum:  Peritoneal fold connecting liver to stomach and duodenum.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

True ligaments of liver:

  • Ligamentum teres hepatis → obliterated umbilical vein

  • Ligamentum venosum → obliterated ductus venosus

False ligaments (peritoneal folds):

  • Falciform ligament

  • Coronary ligament

  • Triangular ligaments

Exam Pearl:
Ligamentum venosum is a true ligament of the liver derived from the fetal ductus venosus.

Anatomy-05.question: ৩৪) Main support of liver -
Anatomy-05.exp:
The hepatic veins are considered an important main support of the liver, as they anchor the liver to the inferior vena cava and posterior abdominal wall. The liver is also supported by its peritoneal ligaments, especially the falciform and coronary ligaments, but these are not the principal mechanical support. The hepatic veins pass from the liver directly into the inferior vena cava, helping maintain the liver's position. Therefore, among the given options, hepatic vein is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Main support of liver → Hepatic veins

Hepatic veins → Drain into IVC

Falciform ligament → Divides anatomical right and left lobes

Coronary ligament → Helps attach liver to diaphragm

Liver is largely intraperitoneal except for the bare area

Exam Pearl: Hepatic veins are the major posterior anchoring support of the liver.

Anatomy-05.question: ৩৫) Kupffer's cells lies in
Anatomy-05.exp:
Kupffer cells are specialized macrophages of the liver located in the hepatic sinusoids.

Functions of Kupffer cells:

  • Phagocytose bacteria, old RBCs, and cellular debris from portal blood

  • Participate in immune defense of the liver

  • Release inflammatory mediators

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Space of Mall:  A periportal space involved in lymph drainage; not the location of Kupffer cells.

  • Space of Disse:  Space between hepatocytes and sinusoidal endothelium; contains hepatic stellate (Ito) cells, not Kupffer cells.

  • Hepatic sinusoid:  Contains Kupffer cells.

  • Hepatic vein:  Drains blood from liver; does not contain Kupffer cells.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Structure Location
Kupffer cells Hepatic sinusoids
Ito (stellate) cells Space of Disse
Bile canaliculi Between hepatocytes

Exam Pearl:
Kupffer cells = liver macrophages = located in hepatic sinusoids.

Anatomy-05.question: ৩৬) Metabolic unit of liver
Anatomy-05.exp:
The hepatic acinus (acinus of Rappaport) is considered the metabolic unit of the liver.

  • It is arranged around the branches of the portal triad and reflects the functional organization of hepatocytes according to their blood supply and oxygen gradient.

  • It is divided into zones:

    • Zone 1 (periportal): Highest oxygen supply, most active in oxidative metabolism.

    • Zone 3 (centrilobular): Lowest oxygen supply, most vulnerable to ischemia and toxic injury.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Portal lobule:  Functional unit emphasizing bile drainage.

  • Hepatic lobule:  Structural unit of the liver, centered around the central vein.

  • Hepatic acini:  Metabolic and functional unit of liver.

  • Hepatocyte:  Main functional cell but not considered the metabolic unit.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Unit Function
Hepatic lobule Structural unit (blood flow → central vein)
Portal lobule Bile secretion/drainage unit
Hepatic acinus Metabolic unit ⭐

Exam Pearl:
Metabolic unit of liver = Hepatic acinus (Rappaport acinus).

Anatomy-05.question: ৩৭) Alkaline fluid containing mucin is secreted from which cell of stomach?
৩৮) Small intestine has
৩৯) Organ with purely serous covering
৪০) I cell secretes
৪১) Main branches of celiac trunk excludes
Anatomy-05.exp:
The celiac trunk has three main branches (classic triad):

  1. Left gastric artery

  2. Splenic artery

  3. Common hepatic artery

The pancreatic arteries are not direct main branches of the celiac trunk. They arise from branches of the celiac trunk, mainly the splenic artery (e.g., dorsal pancreatic artery, pancreatic branches).

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Left gastric artery: One of the three main branches of celiac trunk.

  • Splenic artery:  One of the three main branches.

  • Common hepatic artery:  One of the three main branches.

  • Pancreatic artery:  Not a direct main branch of celiac trunk.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Celiac trunk branches:

  • L → Left gastric artery

  • S → Splenic artery

  • C → Common hepatic artery

Mnemonic: "Liver, Spleen, Stomach"

Exam Pearl:
Celiac trunk has only three main branches: left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries.

Anatomy-05.question: ৪২) Major salivary gland excludes
৪৩) Serous acini
৪৪) During the relative ascent of the kidneys in fetal development, the kidneys rotate
Anatomy-05.exp:
During the ascent of the kidneys in fetal development, the kidneys undergo a 90° medial rotation.

  • Initially, the fetal kidneys are located in the pelvis with their hila facing anteriorly.

  • As they ascend to the abdomen, they rotate 90 degrees medially, causing the hilum to face medially in the adult kidney.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • 90 degrees laterally:  Rotation is not lateral; it is medial.

  • 60 degrees medially:  Incorrect degree of rotation.

  • 60 degrees laterally:  Incorrect direction and degree.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Kidney ascent: Pelvis → abdomen

  • Rotation: 90° medial rotation

  • Final hilum position: Faces medially

  • Adult kidney level: T12–L3 (left kidney slightly higher)

Exam Pearl:
Developing kidneys ascend and rotate 90° medially so the hilum changes from anterior to medial.

Anatomy-05.question: ৪৫) Serous demilune are present in
Anatomy-05.exp:
Serous demilunes (Gianuzzi’s demilunes) are present in mucous salivary glands, especially the sublingual gland.

  • They are crescent-shaped groups of serous cells located at the edge of mucous acini.

  • They secrete enzymes (e.g., lysozyme, amylase) that mix with mucous secretion.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Parotid:  Purely serous gland; no mucous acini, so no serous demilunes.

  • Sublingual:  Mixed gland, predominantly mucous; contains prominent serous demilunes.

  • Buccal:  Minor salivary gland; not a typical site tested for serous demilunes.

  • Submandibular:  Mixed gland but predominantly serous; serous demilunes are less prominent compared with sublingual.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Salivary gland Type
Parotid Pure serous
Submandibular Mixed (mainly serous)
Sublingual Mixed (mainly mucous) + serous demilunes

Exam Pearl:
Serous demilunes are classically associated with the mucous acini of the sublingual gland.
